1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Three Knights Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3.background: Also known as the Kasparov Variation, after Garry Kasparov, who used it to great effect against Anatoly Karpov in their 1985 World Championship match, playing it six times for three wins and three draws.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5.strategy: Attacks d4 at once and keeps the pin on c3, so Black's plan stays clear whatever set-up White chooses. White must decide how to meet the pressure on d4: with a solid pawn on e3 or with a fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6.strategy: Aims for a bishop on b7 to control e4 while the bishop on b4 keeps the pin. Black combines the pin with a queenside fianchetto and leaves the pawn centre for later.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 Bxc3+.strategy: Gives up the bishop before White has spent a move on a3, leaving White the bishop pair and doubled c-pawns. Playable, since the knight is already on f3, but Black has settled the matter unforced and has to prove that the structure outweighs the bishops.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6 5.Bg.strategy: Pins the knight on f6 against the queen, so it cannot leave for e4 without uncovering the queen to the bishop, and adds a second pin to the one on c3. Black has to untangle without giving White a free hand.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6 5.e3.strategy: Solid and flexible: it opens the f1-bishop's path to d3 and builds the centre. White accepts that the pinned knight cannot take on e4, so the black knight may settle there, and plans to challenge it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6 5.Qc.strategy: Guards e4 with the queen and prepares to retake on c3 with it, so ...Bxc3 would not double White's pawns. The queen comes out early and can become a target, and development is still to be finished, but the structure stays healthy.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6 5.Bg.strategy: Asks the g5 bishop at once what it wants: keep the pin by retreating, or trade itself for the knight. Black spends a pawn move but gets a clear answer before choosing a set-up, while the bishop on b4 keeps the c3 knight pinned.

Completes the usual set-up: the bishop on b7 eyes e4 and the long diagonal, the pin on c3 stays, and White's pin on f6 does no harm because the knight is defended. Black fights for e4 and can challenge the g5 bishop at a convenient moment.

Takes the knight at once to double White's pawns, while the bishop on g5 still pins the f6 knight against the queen. White gets the bishop pair for doubled pawns, and Black has to keep an eye on the pinned knight while developing.
Keeps the bishop and the pin on f6 instead of exchanging on f6. The bishop can be challenged by a pawn advance on the kingside, but that advance weakens Black's king, so the position stays tense.

Trades the bishop for the knight and ends the pin at once. The game becomes simple and level: Black recaptures with the queen, which develops with a look at d4, while White has given up a bishop that was doing a job and has no clear plan for more.

Steps out of the pawn's reach and keeps the bishop on an active diagonal, but it gives up the pin on the f6 knight and loses time: Black can hit the bishop again with the knight. A harmless retreat that leaves White without an edge.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6 5.Bg.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Kasparov Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6 5.Bg.strategy: Completes the fianchetto while keeping the pin on the c3 knight, which restrains White's centre. Black now fights for e4 and d5 with pieces and decides later how to deal with the pin on f6. A complex game with chances for both sides.

Breaks the pin at once by attacking the bishop with a pawn. White's bishop normally has to retreat, which frees the f6 knight to jump into the centre, but the pawn on g5 weakens Black's king's side for the rest of the game and makes castling there unattractive.

Gives up the bishop to double White's pawns, the usual Nimzo exchange. The pin on the f6 knight stays, though: the knight cannot move without exposing the queen, so Black still has to solve it, while White has the two bishops and a solid centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6 5.e3.strategy: Plants the knight on e4, where the pinned c3 knight cannot take it, and prepares ...Bb7 to support it. Black fights for the central square before White has built a centre, at the cost of moving the knight a second time.

Completes the fianchetto and aims at the e4 square and the long diagonal while the pin on c3 holds back White's centre. Black keeps every plan open and leaves White to decide how to meet the pressure on e4.

Gets the king to safety before the centre opens and leaves the pin on c3 in place. Quiet and sound: it commits Black to nothing in the centre, but it does not yet put a piece on the long diagonal, so White gets time to finish development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6 5.e3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: St. Petersburg Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 b6 5.e3.strategy: Hits the knight on e4, which nothing protects yet; the pinned knight on c3 cannot take it, so the queen does the work. The queen also guards c3 against the bishop. Black has to support or trade the knight at once.

Unpins the knight, so it can challenge the one on e4. Black can trade on d2 or c3, and White may still end up recapturing with the b-pawn; either way the game stays quiet and level, with White's extra space against Black's solid set-up.

Hits the knight on e4 and covers c3, so Black cannot trade on c3 for free. The queen blocks the king's bishop and can be harassed, though; Black supports the knight or trades it off, and White has lost time.

Guards the knight on e4, which White's queen attacks, and puts the bishop on the long diagonal in the same move. Black keeps the knight on its strong central square and the pin on c3 in place, so White has to spend time challenging the knight rather than developing.

Doubles White's pawns before the queen can recapture: Qxc3 would lose the queen to the knight on e4, so White must take with the pawn. Black gives up the bishop pair, but the knight stays in the centre and White's structure is damaged.

Supports the knight on e4 with a pawn, so the queen's attack is parried without using a piece. The price is a looser king's side and a weakened e6 pawn: Black plays an aggressive, committal set-up in which the knight dominates the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 Bxc3+ 5.strategy: Recaptures with the pawn, accepting doubled c-pawns in return for the bishop pair and a broad pawn centre. The pawns on c3 and c4 are a long-term weakness that Black will attack, but White gets space in the centre and a base for play against the kingside.

Blocks the check but leaves the bishop that took the knight alive: it takes the new blocker with check, and White is a whole piece down for nothing. The check has to be answered by recapturing the bishop.
Blocks with the queen, which the bishop on c3 simply takes with check. White loses the queen for a bishop on top of the knight.

Aims at the c4 pawn, the soft spot of White's doubled pawns, from the long diagonal or from a6. Black fights the pawn mass on the queenside instead of the centre, and White has to defend c4 or hurry with the central and kingside play before the pressure tells.

Blockades the doubled pawns and hits d4 at once, the thematic way to treat this structure. White's pawn mass is slowed; Black goes after the weak c4 pawn with bishop and knight, while White hopes for central and kingside play before the pressure tells.

Prepares ...e5 to challenge White's pawn centre directly and builds a solid structure. Black meets the pawn mass with a compact blockade instead of attacking c4 at once, accepting a slower fight against the weak pawns.

Solid: the pawn supports d4 and frees the king's bishop, which can defend c4 from d3. White accepts the structure, doubled pawns against the bishop pair, and plays to build its centre while Black's queenside pressure is still slow.

Develops with a pin on the f6 knight, so Black's knight cannot move without exposing the queen and ...Ne4 is out. The c4 pawn stays the target, and the bishop can be challenged by a pawn on the kingside, which weakens Black's own king.

Protects the c4 pawn with a piece and prepares to build a broad pawn centre. The price is development: the knight blocks the d-file and the c1 bishop's usual diagonal, so White is slower while Black works against the queenside pawns.

Brings the bishop to the long diagonal, where it eyes the knight on f3 and the e4 square that White needs for its big centre. Black makes it harder for White to advance in the middle and keeps the weak c4 pawn as a target for later play.

Attacks the c4 pawn at once from a6, the other route for the bishop. The pressure ties the king's bishop to the defence of c4 and forces White to find a way to hold the pawn, and the bishop eyes the whole queenside.

Challenges d4 and blocks White's pawns on the c-file, fixing the structure. Black plays against c4 and the loosened queenside with pieces rather than pawns, accepting that White keeps the bishop pair and central space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.g3.strategy: The main reply: White fianchettoes the king's bishop and accepts that the centre may open. If Black takes on d4 and the knight recaptures, the bishop on g2 looks down the long diagonal at Black's queenside and keeps up the pressure there.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.d5.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Three Knights Variation, Korchnoi Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.d5.strategy: Gains space and ends the fight for d4: the pawn on d5 cramps Black's e6 pawn. White gives up the central tension, though, and the pin on c3 stays, so Black has easy play against the c4 pawn that supports the advance.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.e3.strategy: Heads for a solid set-up: the pawn supports d4 and frees the king's bishop, and White castles before deciding how to meet the tension in the centre. Less ambitious than a fianchetto, it leaves Black the choice of how to resolve the centre, and the pin on c3 stays.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.d5.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Three Knights Variation, Euwe Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.d5.strategy: Attacks the pinned knight on c3 at once and claims the e4 square before White can build a centre. White has to defend or exchange the knight, which costs a tempo, and Black gets real counterplay against the d5 and c4 pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.d5.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Three Knights Variation, Shocron Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.d5.strategy: Sacrifices a pawn at once to undermine the c4 pawn and open lines for the queen's bishop. White can take the pawn on b5 or on e6, so Black has to show that the open lines are worth it; it is a risky try rather than a refutation of 5.d5.

Takes the pawn at once instead of letting White cramp the position. The pinned knight on c3 cannot recapture, so the c-pawn must take, and Black gets a queenside pawn majority against White's central one while the bishop pin keeps White's pieces tied.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.g3.strategy: Resolves the tension at once and dissolves White's pawn centre. After the recapture Black develops freely, while White's bishop, once on g2, presses on the queenside in return; this is the main line.
Puts the king away and keeps the pressure on d4 from the c5 pawn. A calm move that leaves it to White to decide how the central tension is resolved, while the bishop pin on c3 stays in place.

Develops a piece against d4 and keeps the tension. Playable but unambitious: it commits the knight before Black knows how White will treat the centre, and it leaves the king in the middle while White completes the fianchetto.
The natural recapture: the knight lands on a strong central square. It also opens the long diagonal for the bishop that will go to g2.
Recaptures with the queen, which is attacked by ...Nc6 and has to move again. Black gains a tempo, and White gets nothing in return for putting the queen in the centre.
Ignores the pawn on d4, which takes the knight on c3 at once. ...dxc3 wins a piece for a pawn, and recapturing on c3 only lets the bishop on b4 take more with check.
Castles before the position opens further. With White's centre dissolved, king safety comes first, and Black can then challenge the centre from a safe position.

Develops a piece and puts the knight on d4 under pressure at once. White has to decide whether to trade it, and Black keeps the pin on c3 and can castle later; the cost is that the king stays in the centre while the long diagonal opens for White's fianchetto bishop.

Doubles White's pawns and removes the knight that guards e4 and d5, the classic Nimzo exchange. White recaptures with the pawn and gets the bishop pair and a broad centre, so Black must prove the doubled pawns are weak; with the king still in the centre it is less accurate than castling first.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.g3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Romanishin Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 c5 5.g3.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and clears the way for castling. White keeps the central tension and counts on the bishop to work along the long diagonal once the knight steps aside.

Asks the bishop to decide at once. If Black takes on c3, White recaptures with the b-pawn and gets the bishop pair at the cost of doubled pawns; if the bishop retreats, White has gained queenside space and ended the pin. It delays the fianchetto, so Black gets time to resolve the centre.

Unpins the knight and prepares to meet a capture on c3 with the bishop, which keeps both bishops and a healthy pawn structure. The price is a tempo and a passive piece, and Black can resolve the centre before White has finished developing.
